title: How to hide cursor in Photoshop on Mac: expert tips for a cleaner canvas
metaTitle: How to hide cursor in Photoshop on Mac (Easy Steps)
description: Learn how to hide cursor in Photoshop on Mac by adjusting settings or using system tools to keep your workspace clear for precise design work.
intro: You cannot completely hide the cursor in Adobe Photoshop because it is essential for tool precision. You can, however, switch to a minimal crosshair view or use third-party tools to hide the pointer during screen recordings.
tldr: Press Caps Lock to toggle between standard and precise crosshair cursor modes.
Go to Photoshop > Settings > Cursors to choose the appearance of your brush tip.
Enable 'Show only crosshair while painting' to reduce visual clutter while working.
Use third-party apps like Cursorcerer if you need to hide the cursor entirely for video recording.

blocks.text: Adobe Photoshop relies on the cursor to represent your active tool. Whether you use a mouse, trackpad, or graphics tablet, the application needs to show you exactly where your brush or selection tool is positioned. Because of this, Adobe does not include a native 'hide cursor' button in the software interface. When users ask how to hide the cursor in Photoshop, they usually want to remove the distraction of the brush outline or they are recording a tutorial and want a clean screen.

The most common reason for a 'missing' or 'changed' cursor is the Caps Lock key. When Caps Lock is active, Photoshop forces the cursor into a precise crosshair mode. Many designers accidentally hit this key while typing shortcuts. If your brush icon suddenly becomes a tiny plus sign, check your keyboard first before diving into settings.
How to change your cursor settings
You can customize how the cursor appears by visiting the Preferences menu. This allows you to balance visibility with precision. Follow these steps to adjust your cursor display:

items: Click on the Photoshop menu in the top bar.
Click on Cursors from the sidebar menu.
Choose between Standard, Precise, or Normal Brush Tip under the Painting Cursors section.
Check the box that says Show only crosshair while painting if you want the brush outline to vanish while you are actively dragging.

blocks.text: The Standard option displays the tool icon itself. The Normal Brush Tip shows the actual size of your brush, which is helpful for retouching or painting. The Precise option always shows a crosshair. Choosing the right setting depends on your current task. For example, when using the Clone Stamp tool, you might prefer the Normal Brush Tip to see your sample area. For pixel-perfect selections, the Precise crosshair is usually superior.
Hiding the cursor for screen recording

If you are creating video tutorials, the cursor can sometimes obscure fine details on the canvas. Since Photoshop does not offer a native way to hide the pointer for recording, you need a system-level utility. Cursorcerer is a widely used, free tool for macOS that lets you hide the mouse pointer with a keyboard shortcut. Once installed, you can toggle the visibility of your cursor even while Photoshop is the active application.

Another approach is to use your screen recording software settings. Programs like OBS Studio or ScreenFlow often have an option to 'Hide Cursor' or 'Remove Mouse Pointer' in the final export. This is often safer than using a system utility, as it ensures your cursor remains visible to you while you work but stays hidden for your viewers.

Sometimes the cursor behaves in ways that feel like a bug. If your cursor is flickering or reverting to a standard arrow unexpectedly, there are a few things to check. First, ensure your graphics processor settings are correct. Go to Photoshop > Settings > Performance and look at the GPU settings. Occasionally, disabling 'Use Graphics Processor' can stop flickering, though this may slow down some AI features.

blocks.text: If you use a graphics tablet, such as a Wacom or Huion, the driver software might be overriding the cursor display. Make sure your tablet driver is up to date. Also, check your Mac System Settings for 'Hot Corners' or 'Accessibility' features that might be interfering with your mouse input. Sometimes a simple restart of the computer clears up persistent cursor glitches.
Best practices for a clean workspace

Instead of trying to hide the cursor, many professional designers focus on clearing the interface. You can press the Tab key to hide all panels, toolbars, and the menu bar. This gives you a much cleaner view of your image. Pressing F cycles through different screen modes, allowing you to work on a black background without any UI elements at all. This is often more effective than hiding the cursor.

If you find the cursor distracting, consider using a second display for your panels. By moving all your palettes to a secondary monitor, your main screen becomes dedicated to the canvas. This reduces the need to constantly move your cursor over UI elements. It keeps your workspace focused and helps you maintain a better flow while editing.

faq.question: Can I hide the cursor in Photoshop permanently?
faq.answer: No, Photoshop requires the cursor to remain visible for tool functionality. You can only change its appearance to a crosshair or use external utilities to hide it during screen recordings.

faq.question: Why is my Photoshop cursor a crosshair?
faq.answer: Your Caps Lock key is likely active. Pressing it once will revert the cursor to its standard icon.

faq.question: How do I make the brush tip show the actual size?
faq.answer: Go to Photoshop > Settings > Cursors and ensure 'Normal Brush Tip' is selected.

task: How to hide cursor in Photoshop on Mac
requirements: Keyboard with a Caps Lock key

steps.name: Check Caps Lock
steps.text: If your cursor is a crosshair, press the Caps Lock key on your keyboard to toggle back to the standard tool icon.

steps.name: Open Cursor Settings
steps.text: Navigate to the Photoshop menu, select Settings, then click Cursors to open the customization panel.

steps.name: Adjust Brush Appearance
steps.text: Select the desired cursor style, such as Normal Brush Tip or Precise, based on your current editing needs.

troubleshooting.fix: Press the Caps Lock key to toggle the cursor back to normal.
Go to Preferences > Performance and try toggling the Use Graphics Processor setting.
